utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Wednesday, July 16, 2008. Good afternoon to the accused, to the Defence counsel, to the representatives of the OTP and to everyone assisting us, including the interpreters. Today we'll proceed with the cross-examination conducted by Mr. Stringer and I'm going to give him the floor immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Counsel. And all the other people who are in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buntic. When we concluded the proceedings yesterday, we were talking about the wording and the language of Article 2 of the amended decision on the establishment of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and particularly your interpretation or your view regarding the territorial or geographic scope of the Croatian community. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if I understand your testimony correctly, it's your assertion, sir, that Article 2 of the amended decision -- and perhaps in fairness I should refer you back to the document, which is in binder number 1 on your right-hand side, Exhibit P 00078. Directing your attention to Article 2 of that decision, Mr. Buntic. It's my understanding that your testimony is that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna did not extend or was not intended to extend throughout the entirety of all these municipalities but, rather, to just parts of those municipalities. Is that a correct statement of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna did not have its borders. Throughout its existence, it never had any borders, and Article 2 that we were discussing yesterday does not extend to cover the entire territory of the municipalities listed here, but only "podrucje," areas of the municipalities listed here, but we explained the difference between the contents of the terms "podrucje" and "teritorija" -- area or territory and territory, respectively, and I don't know if we have to revisit that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I think we do. My first question is this. And I'm just reading your last answer: Talking about areas of municipalities, let's take one of these municipalities, for example, Gornji Vakuf. Are you able to tell us, sir, what areas of Gornji Vakuf fell within the jurisdiction or the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? What areas were in, what areas were out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was even a name that I'm now trying to recall, that was under the control and jurisdiction of the HVO throughout the time that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna existed, so, again, we are not talking about the entire territory of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf but just parts of this municipality, but to be quite frank, I can't remember this at this moment, but I do know that throughout the time that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was in existence, there existed this part of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf, and that's what it was called. I think that there are quite a few documents, other documents, that can be used to ascertain the name but I'm sure that there was a specific name for this part of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So Gornji Vakuf, then, was treated differently than Skender Vakuf, for example, in which the drafters of this document, the decree, in fact, identified specifically the region or the area of the municipality that would apply; in other words, as we discussed yesterday, for Skender Vakuf we have specifically identified a place called Dobratici and similarly with Trebinje we have Ravno that's specifically identified. Would you agree with me, sir, that this part of Gornji Vakuf that you've just referred to is not specifically identified in this decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've said about the parts of Gornji Vakuf, and as for Skender Vakuf, the reason was that Dobratici used to be a separate municipality. They had been constituted as a separate municipality and the same goes for Ravno. So before the restructuring of the municipalities in the former Yugoslavia, Dobratici and Ravno were municipalities and that is why those areas are listed here in parentheses and in the areas of the former municipality of Dobratici and the former municipality of Ravno, Croats were in the overwhelming majority. So they are given here as an example, but I assume that the logic that applied here was that Ravno and Dobratici used to be municipalities before the municipalities were restructured in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I've got a map of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf. We are going to put it up on the screen. It's a map showing Gornji Vakuf in terms of its ethnic breakdown. It's in evidence, Mr. President. This is map number 24, Exhibit P 09276. Now, do you see the map on the screen in front of you, Mr. Buntic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet, no, I don't have it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher can assist with that. And while we are doing that, I know that, Mr. Buntic, I don't expect you to have the numbers in your head, none of us do, but if I were to suggest to you that according to the 1991 census, Gornji Vakuf had a Croatian population of 42.5 per cent, a Muslim population of 55.8 per cent and a negligible Serb population of 0.4 per cent, would you agree with me? Would you agree with me that for purposes of our discussion, the Muslim population of Gornji Vakuf was greater than the Croat -- the Croatian or the Croat population of this municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can confirm that. And as you can see, there was not such a great difference, and some parts of the Vakuf municipality, so parts of or territories or areas of this municipalities had Bosniak majority, while there were other settlements there where Croats were in the majority. So we are talking about parts of the Vakuf municipality, and I think that it indicates why the term "teritorij," territory of municipality was not used but rather the term "podrucje," area or territory. So those were the reasons, because we can see on this example here that we have the municipality of Gornji Vakuf where there is a relative majority of Bosniaks, but in some parts, areas, of this municipality, there is a Croatian majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, sir, that based on the fact that the red areas are indicated as Croatian areas or Croat areas, the green areas are indicated as Bosniak or Muslim areas, that the population in Gornji Vakuf was quite -- was quite interspersed, in other words, there are pockets of Croat and pockets of Muslim habitation which are equally distributed or interspersed throughout that municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's not the way I see it. In the right-hand side of this map, we can see 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 13 Muslim settlements in a compact territory. So there are parts of this municipality that are inhabited almost exclusively by Muslims, Bosniaks, and now the question is where are the 40 odd per cent Croats, 46 per cent Croats? They cannot be just nowhere. And we can see an area in the lower corner which is inhabited mostly by Bosniaks but in relative percentages, there were 40 something Croats there, so we can't say that the municipality of Gornji Vakuf is Bosniak municipality because there is over 50 per cent of them there. That is why the term "podrucje," area, was used because we could not claim the whole territory of the municipality, but we could claim, in light of the composition -- ethnic composition of the population, parts of these municipality -- this municipality, and that's where the HVO was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, so if I understand you correctly, sir, you're telling us that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, in Gornji Vakuf, extended to the little red circles but not to the little green circles?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it appears in the map shown here and as far as I know, the actual situation was similar to the one depicted on this map, so in a certain area or in the whole of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf, up until the time when the Croat-Muslim conflicts broke out, there was a joint defence and resistance to the JNA but once the Bosniak-Croat conflict broke out --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the conflict yet. I'm just asking about the ethnic composition in 1991. Would you agree with me, sir, that the ethnic composition of Gornji Vakuf and numerous other municipalities of the Central Bosnia region that were identified here in this decree on Article 2 were much more mixed, in terms of their ethnicity, Bosniak and Croat, much more mixed than, say, for example, the -- your municipality of Citluk, which I think was around 98 or 99 per cent Croat?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these claims are correct, because if we know that if we are talking about the municipalities in western Herzegovina, that in those municipalities, we have between 95 up to 99 per cent of the Croatian population there, which was not the case with the municipalities in Central Bosnia or in Bosnian Posavina, where the population in any given municipality did not have such a high majority in terms of relative percentages in -- to the benefit of any one ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. One last question on the map. If a Croat lived in one of the little green circles, would that person not be living in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way I see it, the way I interpret it, that might be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. I have a different exhibit I want to show you now. It's resting on top of the binders next to you. It's marked 1D 02011. And while that's being located for you, Mr. Buntic, let me just ask you a couple of preliminary questions. Do you know Mr. Zoran Perkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And who is he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Perkovic has a law degree, and before the war, he lived and worked in Sarajevo. I think that at the first democratic elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was a candidate for the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina and just before the war, I'm not sure about this but I think that he worked in the Ministry of Justice or something like that. After he left Sarajevo, he worked in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the summer of 1993, was he head of the commission for regulations of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the commission for regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the commission for regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you turn to the last page of this document, you see the signature and -- would this appear to be a report that he made on or about the 13th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. I see that this is the report of the commission for regulations, but as I've already indicated, I'm not an expert who could claim with any authority whether this is Mr. Perkovic's signature or not, so that would be a question for a handwriting expert, and I'm definitely not one. Perkovic was the president of the commission for regulations of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. That much is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We've seen a number of reports of other departments, and this appears to be a report of his that is reporting on the activities of his commission from the 1st -- from January until June of 1993. Do you see that in the beginning of the report? On the first page of it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that this period is indicated in the subject line, so that's January to June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What he's doing is giving a list of the activity of the commission on the decrees that it wrote during that period and I want to direct your attention to a couple of those. Looking at number 2 on the list, that's a decree on application of the Law on Water Resources. You see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And does that make reference to the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna using the word "teritoriju"? Do you see the word "teritoriju" there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that and this is obviously a deviation from the definition that exists in the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Well, we cannot regulate elements that are regulated by higher-ranking legal documents and instruments, so we cannot amend what is regulated in legal instruments of a higher rank in those by-laws or regulations that are over a lower level legally speaking. I have already presented to you this decision and the higher-ranking document in this case is the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Then would you agree with me, sir, that number 10 here contains another deviation in that this decree on amendments to the decree on application of the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina also makes reference to the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? That's a "yes" or "no" question. You see the word "territory" there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. Yes, and I can agree. The interpretation and my understanding is the same as the one that I presented earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Is that also true of number 11, Law on Health Care in the territory of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that and it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And also number 13?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that likewise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 18 and also 25 also make reference to the territory of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But the other thing is correct too. There are many regulations where no mention of this is made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that was actually -- you anticipated my next question, Mr. Buntic. It appears to me that the words -- the Serbo-Croatian words "teritoriju" or the words "podrucje" appear interchangeably as though there is no real distinction in the way that Mr. Perkovic is using those words. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with you but I maintain what I've already said, and if you want to prove that, I think that you should find a linguistic expert to obtain from such a person an expert report about the meaning of those words in the Croatian language. I told you what I know based on my knowledge of everyday Croatian parlance. There is a difference between those two terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next exhibit, Mr. Buntic, you can put that one aside, is the one that you looked at yesterday at the very beginning of your testimony on cross-examination, 1D 01607. It's in the fourth binder, and this is the minutes of the 37th Session of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. There is a question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. Stringer, because you're about to move to a different document but I don't think we've quite studied this document enough. Of course I can't speak the language of the witness, but I have the text in front of me. You mentioned item number 11, and here in B/C/S, I see the word "teritorij" whereas now if I look at the English translation, I can't find that again. I find the mention Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So I have a suggestion to make. I realise that you have not come to an agreement with the witness with respect to the use of these words, so could we not ask the interpreters to read out item 11 in B/C/S and then listen to their interpretation, to see if their interpretation corresponds to the translation in English we have in front of us? What would you say of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about document 1D 02011.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think it's an excellent suggestion, Your Honour, and perhaps we could just have the witness read the text itself and then the interpreters in their booths could simply make their interpretation for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In all fairness, to be consistent, I think it would be -- I don't want to waste anybody's time but if you go through all of them, you will see that there is -- sometimes it's there, sometimes it's another word, sometimes there is nothing there. So if we are just going to cherry pick number 11, we should maybe look at number 4 or number 5 or may be look at number 6 as well. And I should also add, for everyone's convenience, that Mr. Perkovic who drafted these laws will be our very next witness. He may be the most appropriate witness to answer all of these questions but I just throw that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my proposal would be to have the witness read number 11 and we can have him read as many of these as you wish. I think the point is, as I've indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe we can do both because we have the text in front of us and when Mr. Karnavas's next witness comes to testify, we can ask him to give us his input on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps just to have some balance I'll choose two, one of each, and if that's not sufficient for the Trial Chamber or Mr. Karnavas, he can propose an additional one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just going to number 11, Mr. Buntic, can you read the text of number 11 for us in your language.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Decree on the application of the Law on Health Care in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In war or in times of an imminent threat of war."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now the other word we have been talking about, "podrucje," is found in number 8. I can't read number 8. Perhaps that would be a suitable one, if could you read number 8 out loud for us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 8: "Decree on the application of the Law on Regular Courts in the "podrucje," territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, in war or in time of an imminent threat of war or the state of war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the portion again, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Item 8, decree on the application of the Law on Regular Courts in the "podrucje," territory, of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, in time of an imminent threat of war or state of war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I will repeat myself because I did this yesterday already. Addressing the interpreters: You may have your own Croatian and I'm not capable of discussing the issue, but we have lengthily been told here that "podrucje" falls to be translated as area rather than territory, and I would be grateful if you would try to comply with this linguistic rule which, for the time, I think, can be called a rule, linguistic rule, of this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Without any intention of putting you argument of yesterday because I do not wish to, but I believe that it is a question of linguistic but also, in a way, not only linguistic but, of course, an important political and judicial question. If my view, the two terminology that is territory and area has been intermittently used, sometimes in one way or in the other. If you take the document which we are talking about and page 2 of the Croatian text, then you will see that on page 2, item 12, here is "podrucje" [B/C/S spoken]. In item 13, it is "teritoriju" [B/C/S spoken]. In number 14, it is again "podrucje." In number 15, "podrucje." In number 16, "podrucje." And then at the same time, in many other instances, you can check otherwise that in the English text there is no -- neither territory nor area but there is only said that community of -- the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. In my view, the interpreters here a bit acted one-sidedly but it is up to them. But then again, we say that in -- I admit that in most of these items, the expression is "podrucje" but again, in item 18, it is [B/C/S spoken] Herceg-Bosna. In -- then again 19, 20, it is "podrucje." Now, 21 it speaks about [B/C/S spoken] so it is about the borders. 22, it is "podrucje." 23, "podrucje." And also 24, and again, in 25, it is again "teritoriju" [B/C/S spoken]. So that is why, in my view, again without any opening of the discussion on the terminology, I would say that that area and territory has been used in most of the instances almost in identical way, identical meaning, and I still believe that it is the situation. But I really also believe that we shouldn't lose too much time on this terminology because as we see it at that given time, the terminology was used in this way and that way, and therefore I do not think that we should fear that we have to find out the real -- I mean we can find out the real meaning of the two expressions which are -- which are rather covering each other. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, Judge Prandler, perhaps the witness could read out number 21 and we could get a translation so the Judges can actually see what is being written on 21 because you see a third variant as well. And, again, we'll have the author of these titles, and he can explain to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, I don't think this is necessarily a pedantic point on the nomenclature that's used. I do firstly applaud with the greatest respect Judge Trechsel's intervention and comment about try to use as much precision as possible, but I don't think this is a matter of simple linguistics. There are substantive issues that may turn on the word used and what actually was in the mind at the time when all of this was taking place. So, Your Honour, I'm sure it wasn't intended by His Honour Judge Prandler to indicate a finding prior to a close of the case. Of course, some clarification of course is useful to all parties but this is very much a live issue and it's an issue that could have significant import to the findings of the Trial Chamber and evidence will be called on this matter as part of our case. I think the constitutional expert that the Defence are calling as a joint witness will speak to this issue as well. So I would emphasise for the record that this is very much a live issue and one of significance in our submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I say something that might be helpful? While this discussion was going on yesterday and today, I Googled the word "podrucje" and got 215 possible translations in the English language. Some of them were phrases but the matches were district, area, sector, domain, and so on and so forth. Yesterday, we heard from His Honour the Presiding Judge that the solution in French was similar to the one in Croatian. I uphold what my learned friend Mr. Khan said. This might be a linguistic issue but it's also a legal issue. It's a point of law. The witness gave his interpretation of the issue. He was there and he knows what the intention on their part was. If the Prosecution believes this to be insufficient or inadequate, then it is -- the burden lies on the Prosecution to lead evidence on that issue. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be of assistance, the witness is here, counsel are here, and they can either approve of what I'm saying or disprove it. When we say the territory of the municipality of Citluk we can go into the land registry book and find the boundaries plotted into that book of the municipality of Citluk and there we can find what the territories, "teritorij." When we say "podrucje," it doesn't have any boundaries or borders; it has not been quantified. And when you say "podrucje" or area of Citluk, you do not necessarily mean the entire territory. It can only be part of the municipality which has not been defined anywhere. The territory of a municipality is something that you will find in the land registry books and when you put together ten areas, you will have a territorial unit. That's why the term "podrucje" was used here because nobody had the intention of plotting borders there. The lawyer is here who had something to do with it and I have some land registry knowledge. Territory is something that is plotted into maps. Territory of a municipality. Whereas "podrucje," area, you can say, well, the area of the Neretva River and you can't know possibly what the extent of the area is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me, please, I have been studying the Croatian language and dealing with it professionally. Let's look at the historical use of the word "teritorij." In all the manuals, textbooks and atlases, territory, "teritorij" is always linked with states, the territory of France, the territory of the United States of America. In the Croatian language, "teritorij" is in terms of its substance always related to something that is legally determined, such as a state, or a municipality. "Podrucje" is used in the Croatian language to denote the area of the euro or of Provence or Herzegovina. In other words, what it denotes is rather the cultural and civilization aspect. The area where Burgundy is grown. It has a different substantially speaking meaning, whether we talk about glaciers, whether we talk about a wine-growing area, et cetera, et cetera. And "podrucje," an area, is a non-defined unit whereas a territory is always linked with, for instance, a state, the territory of a state, the territory inhabited by the French, the territory inhabited by the Germans and so on and so forth. "Teritorij," territory, is a much clearer area which has borders, whereas "podrucje," an area, does not have borders and that's where the whole confusion stems from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Judge Trechsel has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's interesting to hear this round of experts from all sides on the Croat language. I think that the last speaker, because this gets a character of a seminar, has spoken too fast and everything was not set down in the record. Inter alia, I heard the expression, the area of the euro, and that is think is something which has borders and can be determined very clearly, but I think what we can conclude is that linguistics, semantics, are important. They are one element in the interpretation of legal texts but definitely not the only one. And as for me, the Chamber is interested in what the actual situation was, and I think we should concentrate on finding that out. And in this respect, I would like to put a question to you, Mr. Buntic, in relation with number 22 on our list. It is a title which does not refer either to "podrucje" nor to "teritorij," but it's a decree on introducing profit tax for legal entities in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and I take it that this means in the area of Herceg-Bosna, as you say. Now, in Croatian, it's "podrucje." Even better, okay. Now, Mr. Stringer has shown you a map of Gornji Vakuf, the community, and on the map we have seen the town, in green, apparently a Muslim majority, and you seem to have agreed that the green spots do not belong to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. That's the parts that are not covered by this a bit vague expression of area. Now, I suppose there were industrial enterprises, legal entities, in the town of Gornji Vakuf. Were they exempted from profit tax? And if so, how would this -- where would this have been regulated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of a single case specifically speaking about income tax --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Profit tax.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which was of them -- profit tax ever being forcibly imposed on companies through decisions to that effect issued by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or through any other methods. I'm not aware of a single such case. I'm referring to this decree introducing profit tax for legal entities. Again we are talking about "podrucje," an area, but I do stand by what I said, that wherever the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna issued decrees, the term of "podrucje" was used much more frequently than "teritorij" but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm stopping you because I don't want to hear about words. I think there was a certain agreement that words do not lead us anywhere. How about income taxes? Were income taxes paid in the municipalities and/or in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depending on the times, Your Honour, I did say something about it yesterday. In the course of 1992, and most likely in the first half of 1993, none of it was paid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I do not need details, Mr. Buntic. You have implicitly said that in principle, income taxes were levied although not all the time. I'm interested in the levying of the taxes. Was a distinction made of whether someone lived, I simplify, in a green locality or in a red locality, in the sense that in a green locality, which was not part of Herceg-Bosna, you did not have to pay income tax?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we had the head of the finance department, and I ask you to acknowledge the fact, with all due respect, that I did not have many dealings with financial matters, nor am I competent to speak about that. I know very little about the payment of taxes. I asked you to allow me to tell you what I know before you interrupted me. I am doing my best, but this is something I really know nothing of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, the head of the finance department will be coming here and he may be in a better position to give you a precise answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That may well be so but we have this witness who has said a lot about this matter. Mr. Buntic, was it at all of some relevance whether a town belonged to the HVO or not, or was it completely irrelevant, did it make no difference to people? Would you say you don't know either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I was quite clear on that score as well. Wherever the HVO existed and was active in principle the regulations of the HZ HB were applied. Where the HVO did not exist and where there was no actual control in place, taxes were not levied through any forcible methods. I'm not aware of that. And I mean forcibly by employing the military to make sure that, let's say, Bosniak citizens pay their taxes to the HZ HB. I know that up until the second half of 1993, it was predominantly the municipalities that made sure that the taxes were paid, but as Mr. Karnavas said, the head of the finance department will be testifying here soon and he is very familiar with financial issues. This is not my profession, and this was probably the matter that I took least account of throughout the existence of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It seems to have escaped your attention, Mr. Buntic, that in my last question, I did very expressly not refer to taxes but other matters. But you were the Minister of Justice, and you must have known where the laws applied and where they did not apply. Now, how, if I at that time were, for a spurious reason, interested in going to live somewhere in the area of Herceg-Bosna, how would I know where the legislation applies and where it does not apply, within the area concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I must intervene again. I don't know if it was interpreted to me correctly, the word minister was used. I was not a Minister of any sort. I was head of the Justice Department, head of the justice and general administration department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I accept that that was your title but the function was not really very different, but I apologise, I misspoke in this respect. But even as a head of the department of justice, would you not be expected to know where the law -- because we are talking about law, are we not -- decrees, they are norms, binding norms, how did anyone find out whether in one place it applied or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As head of the justice and general administration department, in other words, as head of an executive body, I was charged with the implementation of decrees and all other regulations applicable to justice administration. When it came to these decrees and lower-level regulations, this is an area that I'm fully competent for and I can answer any question which has to do with that, but please spare me the questions about how other departments applied regulations from within their respective fields. In my view, every head of office was responsible for the implementation of regulations falling within his or her own purview. I do not wish to speculate because in that case, I would not be speaking the truth. I'm not competent to speak the truth about these matters simply because I don't have enough knowledge about it. We have the Trial Chamber here, we have the Prosecution, and I believe that all the relevant persons can be called to testify about their respective areas. I have been here for seven days now and I have been answering questions from the Defence and the Prosecution about everything that I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sir, I did not invite you to speculate. I didn't invite you to speak about other departments. You have now just said you were responsible for the implementation of certain decrees. How did you know where they were to be implemented and where they were not to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had the defined purviews of -- or rather territories of municipal courts, district courts, the department of the Supreme Court, district military courts. They were set forth in the relevant regulations and legislation. The territories were clearly defined and it was quite clear, under whose jurisdiction which territory fell. These were the matters that fell within my competence, but as for the decree on taxes and how it was implemented, I'm afraid to err in that area. I have been testifying for seven days now about how the decrees from the field of justice administration have been implemented and I can continue doing so. I don't know about the other areas, I'm afraid, and I don't want to either speculate or say something that isn't true. That wouldn't be proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Let's stay, then, with what you know. There were municipalities and the municipalities had a territory and there were courts and so forth. Now, there must be areas where all that did not apply because it did not belong to Herceg-Bosna, although it was on the territory, but outside the area. That's what we are told. How did you know where were the blank spots on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For instance, I have already been testifying about the municipal court in Mostar so I'll take that as an illustration. It covered the areas of Mostar, Citluk and Nevesinje. This is probably a typical example. The municipality of Nevesinje was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, Citluk was under the control of the HVO, and Mostar was for a part of the time under the HVO control and then subsequently it was split into two parts. You're asking me now how it was implemented. Well, I could do whatever I wanted, but to try and implement the law on regular courts in the area of the Nevesinje municipality would have been a folly. I could not have done that. Who was I or the other two or three associates working with me to go there and try and coax them or force them into accepting the fact that we would now be adjudicating their cases? This was not the way I could have done. I did what was realistically possible. I gave you one example that I believe is quite characteristic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Was Nevesinje on the part of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Then it's not in the area and not in the territory. We are only interested in places which were in the supposed territory but not in the area. And I think I'll leave it at that but it seems that you have not given us any source where it would have been possible to look up in a book, in a register, and say this belongs to the area and that does not belong to the area. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome. Can I now please answer? It is true, however, it's also true, that Nevesinje was part of the territory under the jurisdiction of the municipal court in Mostar and we took over that part of the law as our own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, further to the questions that were put but still something different, we know that Zoran Perkovic will come and testify here. Therefore we will be able to put all relevant questions to him. However, if I correctly understand how the system worked, how those decrees worked, it seems that the commission for regulations which was led by Mr. Perkovic was established and started functioning or functioned between January and June 1993. Based on Mr. Perkovic's report, and we will ask him for some explanation on that report, he states in that report that they had some difficulties to work because there was a president, Mr. Perkovic, and three members in that commission. Among those three members, two were nominated to be -- to become members of the Supreme Court so there were four at the beginning but only two in the end worked. So they ran into difficulties. However, I see that in that commission, there were two legal entities, because those people were nominated to become members of the Supreme Court. From that moment onwards, people who were working on the decrees were supposed to be specialists. Afterwards there was one president and two members. When I found out how this commission was composed, I wondered what the composition was. According to your knowledge, were there Croats and Muslims who were part of this commission or were there only Croats or only Muslims, or was it a mixed composition? How was the commission made up? Because this commission played an important role, it gave advice and contributed to the drafting of texts, we will ask Mr. Perkovic about that. So in coordination with various departments they worked together and afterwards those decrees were supposed to be signed by Mr. Boban. Then at the department level, there was the implementation of those decrees. You managed to implement some of those decrees, including those on the courts. You implemented those decrees. But it seems that most of the job was done by that commission. As far as you know, was this a multi-ethnic commission? Were the members of the commission the ones to whom we should put those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, but I want to highlight the following thing. The Muslim Vahid Vlahovic [phoen] was in the initial period on the commission. Perkovic was appointed only later on. Now, throughout the existence of the HZ HB, the commission had members of Bosniak Muslim and Croat ethnicities. So the presidents also changed. First there was Vlahovic and then Perkovic and throughout that period as members, both the Bosniaks and Croats were represented. If Mr. Perkovic is due to appear as a witness here, then he will provide you with evidence that will be more authentic than what I can give you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. This is very relevant, because now we know that this was a mixed commission, with Croat and Muslim members. But you were in charge of the department of administration and justice, and you implemented these regulations. You were not the one who drafted them. You implemented them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. The regulations that pertained to the judicial system, I was duty-bound to implement them as the head of the department. To be more specific or to simplify matters it was my task to set up a functioning judicial system, a functioning judiciary, so that it could function as a whole. So all the regulations that pertained to that area, it was my duty to implement them and to make sure that the civilian judiciary could function properly and regularly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One final question: In the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, things seemed to be organised along the same lines as what happens in other states. So I'd like to know whether this was a judicial control of decrees. If a decree was found to be going against the law, against the constitution, was there a mechanism in place to challenge this decree on a legal basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. There was an institution, both the republican and the federal court, constitutional court, and there was this possibility. Whoever considered that a regulation or a bylaw was contrary to the constitution or any provisions thereof were contrary to the federal constitution, they could lodge a complaint before the federal constitutional court of Yugoslavia; and if they thought that it was contrary to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then a complaint could be lodged before the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the constitutional court was part of the control mechanism that verified whether all the legal acts, any regulations or by-laws or even statutes of the companies were in line with the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand correctly, the decree could be challenged, thanks to a judicial mechanism. Let me repeat my question because it has not been translated. If I understand correctly, it was possible to challenge decrees, anyone was able to do so, anyone believing that the decree was illegal. There was a mechanism in place to allow for these decrees to be challenged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, did not at one point the constitutional court made a ruling about the legality of the foundation of HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is correct, Your Honour, but I would like to note here that I learned about this decision as late as in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I do not want to challenge this, but how big are the chances that the court, a court, and you have not spoken unless I have misunderstood of another constitutional court, that a constitutional court would declare a decree as lawful if it's the decree of an entity which itself, rightly or wrongly, the court has declared not to be a lawful entity? I see Mr. Karnavas would like to answer the question. I put the question to the witness and I don't think it's an unfair question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's a very fair question. But what is unfair, no disrespect to the Bench, is putting tremendous time constraints on me that I cannot go into issues only for the Bench, then, to take over before the Prosecution even does his cross-examination. These are very legitimate questions. The problem I have is either I choose to put in documents or discuss issues. And you put me in a position where effectively, I'm being ineffective to my client because I don't have time to develop these issues and now you're asking these questions when I should have asked them but I had no time. But I agree with you and I invite to you look at the Kordic trial transcript because that issue was covered extensively through this gentleman. But I just wish to put my marker on, again, because at the conclusion of today's hearing, I want five minutes to renew my request for additional time to put on my case based on what I'm seeing here today. These are legitimate questions, you're entitled to ask them but I should be asking them but I don't have the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I plead guilty. I've been a bit excessive this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Those are good questions. No, these are good questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That doesn't mean that I have to put them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, now these issues have been raised, not to mention only matters of semantics or judicial or legal matters. Well, you will be able to raise these issues with your following witness because considering the position of the -- your next witness, you will be perfectly entitled to answer any questions you might have about this. And if it's not the case, then you may deal with these matters with another witness. There is always this possibility. You can't, with one witness, deal with everything. You have to pick and choose. The Bench also has a lot of questions it could ask the witness, but we try to control ourselves. We try to only go to the heart of the matter, because otherwise we would need weeks, months, and we don't have that time. Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think I can inform that you virtually all the issues that have been touched upon in the last half an hour or so are in my outline. I am intending to raise them as part of the cross-examination. What I'd like to do before the break is perhaps try to finish off, if possible, this last issue on the territorial aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I believe, Mr. Buntic, in front of you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you just said that the matters we have raised are part of the outline -- of your outline. If you had given us your outline, then we would have seen that you intended to put these questions to the witness and we may have decided not to put the questions to the witness ourselves, but we had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. I know that's how it works. In a perfect world, I could give you my outline in advance but that would indicate that I'm probably more organised than I really am. Cross-examination, I think, requires a bit more spontaneity because you don't ultimately know what the questions are going to be until you hear the direct examination, until you hear the witness give you his answers, and so I actually -- I have a plan but it's probably not something that would be of use to you in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Stringer, you're not listening to our good questions and afterwards you invent that you had them in your plan and were going to put them yourself, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's not true because you're going to see the documents in the binders that relate to those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I think that you should have in front of you one of the first exhibits that I showed you yesterday, which is 1D 01607, minutes of the HVO Presidency meeting of 5 May 1993. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this was the document I showed you yesterday in which you and the others had approved the minutes of the earlier meeting of the 35th session, which you had said were erroneous. Do you recall that being the subject?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Very quickly, just turning to the agenda here that's proposed by Dr. Prlic for this, the 37th session of the HVO, would you agree with me, Mr. Buntic, that there are references, numerous references, in this document to the territory, "teritoriju," of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? I'm looking at items 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, of the agenda, as well as item 2 on the next page. And then again it's references to the territory of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna found in items A and B under item 3. So again, I don't intend to cite them all but would you agree with me, sir, that this document makes numerous references to territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? It's a yes-or-no question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a yes or no as my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question is do you see the word territory, "teritoriju," in that document, in these places that I've indicated? Do you see the word there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see this word, but the proper question would be to list all the documents passed by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and then ascertain in how many of those documents one word is used and in how many the other is used. And as I've already explained, if the term territory was used, it was used in contravention of the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, so it was used because -- but it was illegal, unlawful, because it was contrary to the terminology used in the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit I'd like to direct you to is in binder number 4. It is 1D 02253. 2253. Earlier in your testimony, you told us about the Croatian community in Teslic, which is in, I believe, north-central Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there was some text in there, I think you looked at this exhibit during your direct examination, there was some text in there that I found interesting. Could you read for us, sir, the very first paragraph of this document, just read it out loud in your language?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Article 1: The following administrative offices shall be formed to deal with administrative affairs in the 'podrucje,' area or territory of the Croatian part of the municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, you just read Article 1. Which as you've indicated makes reference to the Croatian part. I wanted also, actually, for you to read the very first passage beginning with the words, "Pursuant to the statutory decision," which appear just under the date.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. Yes. I received interpretation to read Article 1 and you want me to read the preamble. "Pursuant to the statutory decision on the temporary establishment of the executive government and administration in the 'podrucje,' area or territory, of the Croatian part of the Teslic municipality, the Teslic HVO, Teslic Komusina HVO hereby issues the following."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So now we see in the preamble and also in Article 1 that the people who wrote this document expressly, explicitly, indicated that the area covered by this decision was the Croatian part of the municipality, the Croatian part. So this is my question: Isn't it true, Mr. Buntic, that had you and the others who wrote that amended decision establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, if you had wanted to indicate in Article 2 that it applied only to the Croatian parts of those municipalities, you could very easily have done so just like the people who wrote this decision in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite apparent that in the decision on the establishment of the HZ HB, and in this decision, the explicit term that is used is "podrucje." So no fundamental act speaks about the territory but -- "teritorij" but only about "podrucje." So these are fundamental legal instruments and all the other legal acts or instruments have to be in line with them, because they are of a lesser rank legally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this document, it refers explicitly to the Croatian part, "podrucje Hrvatskog" [phoen] whereas your decision does not refer to the Croatian part of those municipalities, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do accept this difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, now is a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Mr. Stringer, I would like to turn to Mr. Karnavas. With respect to the following witnesses, we are currently in the following situation. The Prosecutor will probably complete the cross-examination of the witness tomorrow. I do not know how long it will take for you to put your additional questions for re-examination. Then we have Mr. Kovacic who requested six hours for Mr. Perkovic plus three hours for the other Defence counsel, six hours for cross-examination by the Prosecution, that is a total of 15 hours. In other words, next week we can't possibly complete the testimony of Mr. Perkovic because Mr. Zuzul is scheduled to come back on Tuesday, and unless I'm mistaken, he should be cross-examined during five hours. So as things stand now, we may start with Mr. Perkovic on Friday, then we would continue with him on Monday, then we would have Mr. Zuzul because we asked him to come on Tuesday. Then we would resume Mr. Perkovic's testimony and if we can't complete it, then Mr. Perkovic will have to come back in August after recess because I see no way of us being able to complete his examination or his testimony, but you may have some -- something to add to this, some light to shed on this. You may be able to reassure us, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I wish I could reassure you, Your Honours. I can tell you that I am rather dumbstruck at the fact that here we have this gentleman here for such a long time on the stand and yet we are nowhere near finishing him. I understand the Bench has lots of questions. My colleagues on this side took their time as well and asked for additional time. Be that as it may, we are running into a problem. Now, Mr. Perkovic is -- works for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He's not some junior clerk. We have been -- he's been -- he holds very important positions, and the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina has been kind enough and gracious enough to extend his stay here next week, part of next week, because of the importance of this case. However, now I must say that I don't see how I can do both Mr. Perkovic and at the same time bring back Mr. Zuzul if we are going to continue at this pace. Frankly, I don't mind if we spend two weeks with any particular witness or with all the other witnesses. For me it doesn't make a difference. I just -- for planning purposes, however, it does cause me a problem. And I should note that during the Prosecution's case, we wanted witnesses to be in The Hague for extended period of time but we were not accommodated because of course the witnesses have their own particular schedules and we can't force people to stay here longer than they want to stay. I need to do some thinking. I certainly don't want to put on Mr. Perkovic only to bring him back. I can tell you witnesses are not happy when they are here for a long time waiting. I can also tell you, and I don't think that the Judges fully appreciate this, that every day I have to get ready, which means every day I get up at 4.00 to get ready and it's like I'm getting ready for a race that I never get to run. And there is the adrenalin rush and then there is the adrenalin rush down and every day I'm having to re-prepare and I can tell you, it is exhausting. I'm not complaining I'm just telling you how this works for those of us who really take this job seriously. I will just need to do the numbers and see whether we can do Mr. Perkovic. I certainly don't want to start him only to bring him back again because, one, it gives the Prosecution more time to dig up stuff and I understand that they do actively do that and that's their -- I would do the same thing. That's number 1. Number 2, I don't want to inconvenience the gentleman any more than I have to. With respect to Mr. Zuzul, I don't think that we could again call him up and say, you know, how is your schedule in the fall? So I will have an answer for the Court -- tomorrow is what, Thursday? Thursday. I can have a -- I'll have to meet with the next witness, Mr. Perkovic, and ask him and see what his -- how accommodating he can be. I can certainly tell you that it's not a comfortable feeling having to tell a witness this kind of bad news. So any way, but I will do my very best and I will see. We have 120, 130 documents approximately. We are trying to narrow them down. We thought we might be able to do the gentleman in four or five hours. It's almost impossible, especially when I hear the questions from the Bench and the questions are legitimate questions. These are important questions. These are issues that I think should have been raised a year and a half ago but they weren't. Now we are raising them. So I don't want to short change Dr. Prlic. I don't want to rush through this but I will have to get back to you Your Honours tomorrow because I just don't want to make a snap decision. We don't do this, I have to consult with Ms. Tomanovic, she's the backbone of the Defence team even though you probably don't notice it and I don't make decisions without consulting with Ms. Tomanovic. And, of course, I have to consult with Dr. Prlic who also is very engaged in assisting in his own defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, with respect to Mr. Zuzul, as you know he's scheduled to arrive on Sunday by plane. If we decide to postpone his testimony to August and September, we should notify him immediately because he's probably packing at this very minute. It's Wednesday today. If we tell him that we are going to postpone his cross-examination to August or September, we have to notify him immediately because he probably has commitments or he may go on vacation in September. So if you decide that Mr. Zuzul is not going to come back next week, he should be notified as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree with you. And my preference would be to deal with Mr. Zuzul now that he's already set the time aside, but perhaps I can get back to you after the break. I don't want to make any rash decisions at this point in time so we will either decide to postpone Mr. Zuzul, if he's accommodating, if he's able to accommodate us, that is, otherwise we will take him. And then I will have to deal with Mr. Perkovic and see whether we either are going to postpone him until after the break or truncate it. I don't know at this point in time and I don't want to be in a position where I make a decision, I make a promise and then I don't keep it. We are very deliberate in our approach, extremely deliberate. We spend a lot of time putting this case together. It may not show it but we have. And I just need to do the numbers, I need to look at the documents, I need to consult with my team, and so at least with Mr. Zuzul let me have until the next break to try to figure something out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, just one additional explanation since we are now trying to agree how we are going to work until the beginning of our summer recess. When we are talking about Mr. Zuzul I have had the feeling that we only keep in mind the cross-examination for the -- by the Prosecution, and let me remind you that the Petkovic Defence already started its cross-examination, that we were ceded time by other Defence teams and according to my records, we have slightly less than two hours left. I can try to cut down my cross-examination as much as possible in order to contribute to the expeditiousness of our dealings with this witness but please bear in mind that the Petkovic Defence has to cross-examine too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have overheard this or, rather, not heard this but please keep in mind that once Mr. Buntic is done as the Defence witness called by Prlic, we will have some more time for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's why I asked the question. Okay, Mr. Buntic, how are you? Are you all right? Because two weeks, that's quite a long period of time, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to follow up on the last discussion, it's not that it is a major factor, I think the Prosecution's view would be that if we were able to finish the testimony of Mr. Zuzul before the summer break so that he doesn't have to come back later, that would be preferable to having him extend out a longer period of time in order to accommodate Mr. Perkovic. So, again, we understand all of the scheduling difficulties that counsel is encountering but I think we certainly would like to finish off the one witness who is already begun his testimony before we begin another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, just a quick question and it doesn't relate to a document, although if you want to go back to the amended decision establishing Herceg-Bosna, you can go look at that, but we have been talking about Article 2, which has the listing of the municipalities and I understand that you were not involved in the drafting of the original decision from November of 1991 on the establishment of Herceg-Bosna. You were involved in drafting the amended decision. What do you know about the selection of the municipalities that are listed in Article 2?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the criterion for the decision to list those municipalities in Article 2, the areas of those municipalities? I cannot tell you with any certainty but on the basis of the criteria or, rather, the structure of those municipalities, I think that these are the municipalities where Croats are in the relative majority or at least the second-largest population there. So if you analyse those municipalities, if you analyse the ethnic composition of the population there, I think that these were the criteria, so I cannot really be 100 per cent certain, but I can say with some degree of certainty that this was the criterion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before the next question, Mr. President, if Ms. Tomanovic could be excused from the courtroom to sort of take care of some technical issues regarding the last matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, are you familiar with the concept of what we all call the Croatian Banovina, the area that was formed in 1939?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I do have some knowledge of that, but I will also like to state before this Trial Chamber that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was not -- did not cover the same area as the Croatian Banovina, as you can see from this document, the last document that we looked at. I don't want to go into any other documents but the last document we had, the decision establishing the departments for the Teslic Komusina municipality. The second example would be Usora, the third example would be the Croatian Community of Soli, so Zepce, areas that were nowhere near close to the borders of the Croatian Banovina. Not only were they not part of the banovina, they were also not close to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I understand that those areas up in the north and the east of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Soli, Teslic, Posavina, those did not fall within the territory or the area of the 1939 banovina, but I'm not talking about those. I'm talking about the municipalities listed in Article 2 of the decision establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I'm not talking about any of the other Croatian communities. Herceg-Bosna, is it true, sir, that the selection of those municipalities was related or based significantly on the territory of the Croatian Banovina of 1939?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. The next document that I want to direct you to is in binder number 1. It's Exhibit P 00289. And just to introduce the document, we are -- we started with, and we are still looking at a couple of the documents that come from the Presidency meeting that occurred on the 3rd of July, 1992, and this is another of the decrees that was issued during the course of the Presidency meeting that occurred on 3 July of 1992. So do you have that document in front of you, the decree on armed forces of the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And were you involved in drafting this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of the group drafting this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, a couple questions about various parts of this. Directing your attention to Article 1, well, first of all, let me ask you this: This decree on armed forces, was this document intended to regulate the organisation of the military side or the armed side of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in Article 1, it provides that the decree regulates the rights and the duties of citizens and competencies of the Croatian Defence Council, administrative bodies and legal entities and defending the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Now if you skip down to Article 3 you'll see another reference to territorial integrity of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And the concept or the term is used elsewhere in this document. But let me just ask you -- I'm looking at Article 36 as well, although you don't have to -- you don't have to look at Article 36, if you'll accept my representation. Now, Judge Trechsel asked you a couple of questions getting to the issue of the legislation of Herceg-Bosna and what parts of the territories or the areas the legislation would apply to. My question is an analogous question and that's this: Based on your description of the territory or the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, it seems to me, sir, that the military component of the HVO would not know or would have difficulty even in knowing what territory it's supposed to be fighting for and defending. Would you agree with me, sir? Based on your definition of territory?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would, in part. However, at the same time, I stated before this Tribunal that municipal staffs and municipal HVOs were set up. In other words, these were organisational units of the Croatian Defence Council in certain areas of municipalities. Where the HVO was established for the area of the entire municipality or for an area of the municipality where Croats were the predominant population, those areas were considered areas of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna regardless of whether they were included in or listed in Article 2 of the decision establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, because based on the evidence led before this Tribunal, it is quite evident and clear that there existed areas of municipalities which were not listed in the decision establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, but which at a later date, joined the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Let me remind you and this Honourable Trial Chamber that Article 252 of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which imposes not only the right but also the duty and the obligation of every people and every member of ethnicity to defend the territorial integrity and independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In other words, it is not only a constitutional right but also an obligation on the part of every people to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina and its territorial integrity. The HVO, according to that constitutional -- it had to comply with the constitution. This was a provision of the constitution which was an obligation on the part of the citizens. It was a constitutional norm, not some inexistent law. And the most -- or the strictest of penalties were prescribed for its violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as you said in your direct testimony, sir, this obligation under the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina applied at the municipal level, correct? Municipalities had an obligation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipalities had, but also every people and every ethnic minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had the duty, not only the right, to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the obligation and the unit was at the municipal level, not at the parts of the municipal level, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Once again, though, I'm invoking Article 252 of the constitution where such an obligation is laid out on the part of the people as such, not only citizens. Article 252 of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina is very precise and clear in its terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that this decree on armed forces that we are looking at makes no such distinction as between municipalities or parts of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And going back to that map we looked at a little while ago of the ethnic composition in Gornji Vakuf, now, again, just from the military aspect, what parts of this municipality were covered or subject to the terms of this decree on armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm afraid I might make a mistake by delineating the areas where there were Bosniak or Croat individuals or armies. For instance, I couldn't recall a moment ago what the situation was in Gornji Vakuf. I believe that the HVO was in Uskoplje. I couldn't remember the name of the village before. So I dare not draw the line separating the areas controlled by the HVO on the one side and the BH Army or the Muslim side on the other. I believe that the Tribunal will have an opportunity to hear witnesses on this matter. I placed myself at the disposal of this Tribunal and of the Prosecution to answer all the questions about the army for the period while I was a member of the army, until the 20th of June 1992, and to answer all the questions about the fighting and the conflicts in that area until the 20th of June, 1992. Beyond that, I am afraid I could only provide answers that could be prejudicial or detrimental to either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, is it your testimony, then, sir, that the terms of this decree on armed forces only applied to the territories held by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, there was no possibility in reality to have it apply in other areas. We could have written whatever we wanted, but the fact of the matter is that one has jurisdiction over the part of an area where one is able to exercise one's powers, where such powers cannot be exercised or enforced, you have no jurisdiction in that area, regardless of what the regulations might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Article 3 also makes reference to the citizens of the Croatian community?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I believe it is only a question of translation that the witness mentioned that I placed -- and I quote, "I placed myself at the disposal of this Tribunal and of the Prosecution to answer all the questions about the army for the period while I was a member of the army, until the 20th of June 1992." And then it is continued. I wonder if is it correct that you were a member of the army until 20th of June, 1992? It is what you have said, because I believe you left the army before that, but I'm not sure. I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I answered that question already, and I believe I was quite clear at the time. My formal appointment to the post of the head of the justice and general administration department took effect on the 15th of May, 1992. I also said at the time that I requested that I be allowed to discharge my military duty until such time as the Lipanjski Zora action was completed, because I had already taken part in the preparation of the action. This is the action where Mostar, Stolac and a large part of Herzegovina was liberated. The action ended sometime around the 20th of June at which time I reported for my duty as head of the justice and general administration department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buntic, it was then my fault that I didn't remember exactly about the month. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I wanted to ask you about the reference here to citizens of Herceg-Bosna. Who were the citizens? Were they the people living in the green dots, the red dots, or all the dots? Were they the people living within the entirety of a municipality or just a part of a municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I believe we are running in circles because you keep coming back to the questions the answers to which I believe I've already given. You can put hundreds of questions to me and I will give you the same answers hundreds of times, the same or similar answers. I told you that I am not able to draw the borders of Herceg-Bosna for you and tell you that these were the borders of Herceg-Bosna, when Herceg-Bosna did not have any borders and they did not exist. I cannot do that because they simply did not exist. I find this quite unbelievable, frankly. Borders did not exist and I was quite clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps there may be some misunderstanding. If Mr. Buntic could read in Croatian what Article 3 starts to say because as I'm told, it doesn't say citizens. It says residents. And I do believe that there is a distinct -- this is what I'm told by Ms. Tomanovic but I think there is a -- well, I mean, this is her language. So ... but if Mr. Buntic could read it that might clear up some of the misunderstanding that's going on right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, would you read the first sentence of Article 3 out loud in your language, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We don't have the text on our screens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Every citizen of the HZ HB shall have the duty to protect and defend the independence and territorial integrity of the HZ HB and in particular" --
