utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And just would you read the first sentence of Article 4?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies but let me not testify. Can the witness state the difference between the word "gradjanin" and "stanovnik"? "Gradjanin," citizen, and "stanovnik," resident, or between "drzavljanin," national, and "stanovnik," resident.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before the witness does that, Mr. President, I'm going to object. We've got highly skilled, professional people interpreting for us in the booth who have done this in this case, who have translated the documents in this case for years. They are the ones who decide what are the words. It's not counsel and it's not the witness, and I'm sure Mr. Buntic as someone who has organised courts would agree. It's not the witnesses and the parties who decide what are the words. It's the professionals in the booths. We are getting the words from them and no one else. And I think we have to accept that even if we don't like the words that we get.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, I have to object to what the Prosecutor just said. I have to object because with all due respect for the interpreters, they are not lawyers. Words are of utmost importance to us lawyers. The legal meaning of the word "drzavljanin" and "gradjanin" in my language is different. There is a large difference in legal terms. I'm not saying that the interpreters are poor interpreters but this can be of utmost importance for us lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really would like to refrain from testifying but I have to give my full support to what my learned friend has just said. All due credit to the interpreters but they are not lawyers. We know what the legal meaning of certain words is. In the Croatian language, if this regulation wanted to refer to the word "drzavljanin," national, then they would have used that word. They used a different word, which has broader meaning and includes residents among other things. Our legalese does not speak of -- [In English] citizenship then there is a specific term, legal term "drzavljanin." This term is not used here. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: What does the term mean, then? I mean, Witness, can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, no. I think you're not the witness. I'm sorry, I still know the difference although it's getting late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you provide us with an answer? Because in French, because the French language is very subtle. A citizen and a resident is not the same, so how would you define the word "gradjanin" as mentioned in Article 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a very material difference. The word "gradjanin" has a far broader meaning, and scope. For instance, in the Croatian language, if we say "gradjanin," that can mean a person who lives in a certain town. "Gradjanin" can also mean a member or a resident of a municipality. "Gradjanin" is a broad term used in -- as part of the phrase "svi gradjanin," "all gradjani," meaning the community at large, whereas the term "drzavljanin" is a purely legal term. It has its legal meaning, which denotes a member who has the citizenship of a certain state. So this is a strictly legal term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please spell the word -- the second word that you used, which denotes that it is a legal term applying to a national -- the national of a state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D-r-z-a-v-l-j-a-n-i-n. I don't know if I have to repeat what I said about that word. In legal terms, this word denotes a member of a state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's use an example. If you have a Japanese living in Citluk, that individual would be qualified as a "gradjanin," right? We agree on that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If a Japanese lives in Citluk, then that individual would be "gradjanin" of Citluk but "drzavljanin" of Japan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. And he would be liable to military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In practice, nobody has ever compelled a Japanese, not even a Bosniak or a Serb, to serve in the HVO. I'm not aware of a single such case. But I am aware of -- and I know of -- numerous volunteers of both Serb and Muslim ethnicities who joined the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We are not talking about volunteers. We are talking about a legislative text and what it means and we are not talking about borders either. I think we have been a bit led astray. I don't know what this difference in terms means. But we have legislation which is the basis for a duty to do military service. And you have told us that even between Citluk and Ljubuski they were jealous and only people from their own municipality were called to do military service. Do you agree? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, and this is the way things worked for a long time while the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna existed. The mobilisation was organised by each and every municipality on their own initiative and they had their own commands, respective commands. This decree was intended to organise things differently, to set up a joint staff which would be able to command over all these armies. Such a possibility had not existed before this decree was adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think the Prosecutor should go on and perhaps ask the question again because the answer was to a question that was not asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me try to ask a similar question. I'm going to try to avoid terminology that is subject to confusion or dispute. Setting aside the word citizen or resident, and setting aside whether or not the legislation was applied or implemented, I want to talk about the intention of this legislation, and to whom it applied. Did the decree on armed forces apply to Muslims living in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of the definition contained in the decree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decree speaks of citizens, not of ethnicities or anything else. If we interpret it the way it was written, and as it is, then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So it applies to Muslims living in Herceg-Bosna. But as you've indicated, Herceg-Bosna here, as you're using the term, applies only to Croatian or Croat areas within municipalities, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and I did speak along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So again, going back to Gornji Vakuf as an example, a Muslim who is living in a red circle is subject to the decree on armed forces, but a Croat who is living in a green circle is not subject to the decree on armed forces? Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't state anything of the sort. This is a new question and a new topic. I have so far given no answer on that matter. This is something new. I said what the contents of the decree are, the way it has been written. I told you that I cannot speak about Gornji Vakuf, where the fighting was, where Croats lived or where Bosniaks lived. You have the map in front of you. I cannot speak to that. I cannot speak in terms of green and red dots. What would have happened had we not issued the decree? Why don't you answer -- why don't you put that question? The Defence did not put that question. Why don't you? What would have happened had we not issued this decree? The entire Bosnia-Herzegovina would have been occupied and everything would have fallen through. We have prevented the aggression in part of the territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This question would answer many of the questions you have, not the one you put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you and I have different views of what's relevant and important to the Trial Chamber. I'm entitled to ask my questions to you, and as a witness it's your duty, sir, to answer them. And with respect, sir, it's not you who decides what I'm to ask or it's not for you to decide what's relevant. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree but it is my right to provide an answer and many times you bereave me of that right. You interrupt me and then you go back to what you never allowed me to answer. So, this has happened a number of times, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you were the head of the department of justice and general administration for Herceg-Bosna, you were present at the Presidency meeting on the 3rd of July, 1992, you told us that you were involved in drafting this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And yet, sir, it seems to me that you cannot tell us who fell under the terms of this order, who were the people that it applied to.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the "gradjani" of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Mr. Prosecutor, this is what it says in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may take the opportunity just to mention one thing, Mr. Perkovic has indicated that he cannot be available all next week, and therefore, I think it would be best to make arrangements for the gentleman to leave tomorrow. It might be good to contact the Witness and Victims Section so they can make arrangements for the gentleman to go. Having said that, I know that the other gentleman who is about to testify on Monday, he's coming in on Sunday, but I believe he's flying over the Atlantic. It would be my request that perhaps on Monday -- I know we scheduled all day but if it's at all possible it might be more prudent to start in the afternoon because I do know that it's a lengthy flight and taking the stand, being under oath, being under pressure, and then, of course, we do have all the way until Thursday so there'll be plenty of time. But that's something for the Trial Chamber to consider with respect to Mr. Zuzul, but I would most respectfully request for Mr. Perkovic to be allowed to go and arrangements to be made for his departure tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, so your wish is for Mr. Perkovic to go now and he will come back here at a later date, that you will organise with him. Then we won't be sitting on Monday morning to hear Mr. Zuzul. Of course, he will be jet-lagged. I can understand that very well. And we'll start in the afternoon on Monday. I'm going to turn to the registrar to ask him to get in touch immediately with the Victims and Witnesses Unit for Mr. Perkovic to be able to go home very soon.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could just to make sure I understand, we understand correctly, Mr. Perkovic will be leaving, he'll come back at another time. Mr. Zuzul will begin his testimony on Monday afternoon and after he's finished his testimony next week, then we will be on summer recess?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. And that won't be too soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, if I could ask you to turn to Article 11 of this decree on armed forces, one quick question: There is a reference here to the General Staff as being established within the Defence department. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't see this in Article 1. I do apologise. I don't know what Article you are referring to. I got interpretation -- the interpretation I got indicated that you want me to look at Article 1 and you probably meant another Article.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Article 11.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. That's the interpretation I got now. Article 11 would read as follows: "For the --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's okay. You don't have to read it. If you can just take a look and tell us there is a reference to the General Staff being established within the Defence department. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would appear to be the case, if we look at this Article.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall that was the case that the General Staff of the military side of the HVO was within the jurisdiction of the Defence department?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in practice. This decree was amended by the decree on the armed forces of the 17th of October, 1992, which means that it was in force for a very short time only and I would say that it was implemented to a small extent because it was quite soon amended or supplanted by the other decree of the 17th of October, 1992, but I can say that the Main Staff never functioned in practice as part of the Defence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you could turn to Exhibit P 00303, which should be in the same binder. Again, Mr. Buntic, this is another decision from the Presidency meeting of 3 July 1992. This is amending the original decision on the establishment of the HVO as this executive body. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So just to sort of recap where we are in terms of the organisation of the governmental structures of Herceg-Bosna, this document now indicates that the HVO is the supreme executive and administrative body in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm looking at Article 7 now, on the composition of the HVO of the HZ HB, that it's to be comprised of a president, vice-presidents, department heads and others. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Am I -- is it correct, sir, that at this particular point in time, July of 1992, we did not have vice-presidents, either of the HVO or of the Presidency? The vice-presidents of the HVO came later in October?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We only got the president after the session of the 14th of August, 1992, and the vice-presidents after the session of the 17th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And again, just to take a quick step back, Mr. Boban is still, at this point in time, the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, he is also the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna, and at this time he's also president of the HVO, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now if I could direct your attention to Article 9 of this document, regarding the HVO, let me ask you first, Mr. Buntic, were you involved in drafting the amendment of the initial decision on the establishment of the HVO? Were you involved in the drafting of this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in the drafting of this document, but as I've already said, I was given this document on the first day when I assumed my duties so that was around about the 20th of June. So this document was then handed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Article 9 here states that the HVO president shall be in charge of the work of the HVO and shall be held accountable for it. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday I asked you, we were looking at the initial decision establishing the HVO, and that other decision had a reference to the collective nature or collective responsibility of members of the HVO. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it involved both the individual and the collective. We can look at the document, but I think that's how it was defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And in this document, it appears that there is a shift or a change in the language indicating here that the president is accountable for the work of the HVO, there is no reference to a collective aspect, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Article 9, yes, that's correct. The contents of Article 9 are as you've just presented them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And now, as you've just indicated, it was at the following session in August of 1992 that Mr. Prlic, then, was appointed to be the president of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then just to get a head a little bit in the subsequent, the final meeting of the Presidency, in October, 17th of October, 1992, Mr. Valenta and Mr. Zubak and one other individual, I think Mr. Ivankovic were appointed to be the vice-presidents of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. They were appointed as vice-presidents. Mr. Valenta in principle operated as the head of the HVO for Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with me, sir, that Article 9 here applies and governs the work of the HVO from this point on the 3rd of July, 1992, until the end of the Croatian Community in August of 1993, when the Croatian Community became the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to apologise for something. This document that I have in front of me is the document dated the 3rd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the one? But I have to say that at first, when I was shown this document, I thought it was the decision of the 15th of May, and that's why I said that it was handed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document dated the 3rd of July, and it is quite apparent that this is the document that we are talking about, so what I said before, it could not be handed to me on the 20th of June because it bears the date of the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. So -- I understand that. Are you telling us that this is one of the decrees that you were involved in drafting as part of the Presidency meeting of 3 July 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And would you agree with me, sir, that this document, to the extent it describes or establishes powers and competencies and a system of organisation to the HVO HZ HB, that this is the document that applies to the HVO until the HVO essentially passes on its authorities to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we will have another document regulating the internal structure or organisation of the Croatian Defence Council, and I think that this document should be seen in the context of that document. And that those two documents regulate the jurisdiction and the purview of the Croatian Defence Council and of its departments. So it is not only this document. There are two documents that have to be looked at, the interrelation between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to be asking you about a couple of other documents which relate to the municipal authorities and also the rules of procedure of the HVO. Are those the documents that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think its title is the decision on the structure of the HVO and its departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Just quickly turning to Article 20 here of this document, the amended decision on the HVO of the 3rd of July, 1992, this document in item number 6, Article 20, refers to your department, the department of justice and administration?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the next document that I'd like to show you, I believe, is in binder 4. It's Exhibit number 1D 02261. And the usher will assist you in getting to that one. This was one of the decisions that came from one of the other Croatian communities that you talked about in your direct testimony. This is the statutory decision to establish the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Bosanska Posavina. Do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what caught my eye in this one is part of Article 2 which explicitly states that the Croatian Defence Council is to comprise members of the Presidency of the HZBP, presidents of Crisis Staffs of the municipalities that join, and then a representative of the Muslim people from each municipality and also representatives of legal and legitimate organs of civilian authority of the community. Would you agree with me, sir, that this is a significant difference from the structure of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in that this instrument explicitly provides that there must be a representative of the Muslim people from each municipality as part of the HVO for the Bosanska Posavina whereas there is no such requirement for the Presidency of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with you. In my testimony before this Trial Chamber, when I was shown this decision, I don't know whether this was recorded in the transcript, and in what way, but I think I stated that I considered those solutions to be much better and more fortunate than the solutions contained in the statutory decision or, rather, the decision to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This was a much broader and clearer and more precise document, and I think that this orientation of the Croatian Community of Bosnian Posavina, also in terms of its internal structure, opted for some better and more fortunate solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. That's an interesting point you raise, Mr. Buntic, because I haven't really asked you, you know, your views today versus the views or the intentions as they appear in the documents that were being written back in July of 1992. And we could go back to the decree on armed forces and you can look at it, if you want to, but maybe it's not necessary. I'll just put my question to you and then you can look at the document again if you want. I'm looking at Article 43 of that initial or that decree on armed forces from July of 1992, which provides that the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna have their flag, and this Article specified that the flag was to be the historic tri-colour Croatian flag of red, white and blue, and the historic coat of arms which I think we all would recognise as the very sort of classic or emblematic symbol of Croatia or of Croatian people. My question is whether in retrospect or even at the time you think that a Muslim person in Herceg-Bosna might have had difficulty joining a military organisation which had that as its flag? Don't you think such a flag is a bit provocative under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you asked me a mile-long question and I guess you want me to give you a "yes" or "no" answer. That's not the way I can answer your question. And now I'm asking you: How did every Croat in Bosnia-Herzegovina feel when the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at its session on the 4th of -- 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, and 8th of May, 1992, invited the occupying force, the Yugoslav People's Army, to intervene in Bosnia-Herzegovina and to protect the Croat and the Bosnian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina? By that time it had already occupied large areas of the country. I have this document in my bag. They were fighting under the Yugoslav flag. Could I get any Croat to fight under that flag, the Yugoslav flag? That's not true. The coat of arms is an emblem that is used to designate all Croats throughout the world, not only -- it is not only an emblem of the Republic of Croatia. The coat of arms that we used had the -- another mark that made it different from that used in Croatia. Bosniaks could no longer fight under the Yugoslav flag. Every country, every armed force, has its insignia, and the HVO had its insignia. Nobody is trying to hide the fact that the HVO was a predominantly Croatian force, but there were 30 per cent Muslims, Bosniaks, who were fighting under this emblem, under this flag, until the Croat-Bosniak conflicts broke out. Up until that very moment. But the Bosniaks and Croats did not want to fight under the Yugoslav flag and globe could make them do that, to fight under -- bearing those insignia including the five-point star. They did not want to take part in that. They did not want to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, my question relates to the choice of that particular emblem. I'm not going to argue with you about your apparent -- your rejection of the Yugoslav flag. My question is more in terms of the choice of the Croatian emblem and whether that implies a rejection or a discouragement of non-Croat people from joining the HVO and participating in the organisation and the functioning of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's been asked and it's been answered and you have to look at the period and the time when we are talking about. And I think it's necessary to move on. I think Mr. Stringer got his answer. We could be here for the next hour discussing the same matter. But Mr. Buntic was very clear. We were not going to get Croats or Muslims to fight under the Serbian or the Yugoslav flag while the Yugoslav army was occupying one-third of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I've accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He's been asked and it's been answered. You also indicated 30 per cent, 30 per cent, not 1, not 2, not 10, not 20, 30 per cent of the HVO were Muslim. Obviously, they felt comfortable. What Mr. Stringer fails to ask is what about the Green Berets, what about the Patriotic League, what about the Muslim army? They had their own units. So let's put it into perspective. Let's be fair, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness wanted to add something. Yes, witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to answer this question. So, Mr. Prosecutor, real life and practice provided answers to your question, and the facts and real life situations show that the 30 per cent Bosniak Muslims were in the HVO ranks. So practice showed that they fought, that they wanted to fight. These are facts, not some fabrications on my part, real-life facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. The next exhibit is in binder number 1. It's P 00391. And Mr. Buntic, while those -- while that document is being found for you, let me just tell you what this is about. We are moving on now to the Presidency meeting of the 14th of August, 1992. And I'm going to be giving you a document which your version does not appear to be a complete one, so I'm just going to tell you that right off the bat. Sorry, it's binder 2. I apologise. Mr. Buntic, you'll see it starts at page 9 but if you go to the end of the document, I think you'll find sufficient indications there that these are the minutes of the Presidency -- or part of the minutes of the Presidency meeting of the 14th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's fine. I believe that that's the document. It's the minutes from the meeting of the 17th of October or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have this as the minutes of the 14 August 1992. If you look at the second-to-the-last page, this is 391, if you see the signature page, if you keep turning pages forward to the signature page at the end, if you look at the top -- no, I think you had it already, if you go back one more -- if you look at the top you'll see a date there.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. I can see the 14th of August and the signature below.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this appears to be signatures of all the people who attended this particular Presidency meeting in August.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that these are the signatures of the persons listed here who attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So these would be people who had come from throughout various regions of Bosnia-Herzegovina down to Grude to attend this Presidency meeting, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the first column lists municipalities, the second the first and last names of the persons who represented these municipalities and attended the meeting on behalf of these municipalities, whereas the third column has the signature whereby the persons certify their attendance of the meeting. We can see, on the next page, that in addition to these individuals who represented the 29 municipalities, there are also signatures of other attendees of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm seeing at this meeting you had some gentlemen who came from Sarajevo to attend, Mr. Maric and Mr. Huterer and a Mr. Uspor; is that correct? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I would just -- we have covered a lot of what I had intended to ask you about in this document already. If I could just direct you to item 14, items 12, 13, 14 in the minutes, which I believe is at page 12 of your version, the original-language version. First of all, we had a lot of -- it's my understanding, sir, that there are a number of decrees and legislation that was passed or enacted at this Presidency meeting. Is that -- do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then in these particular items that I've directed you to, items 12 and 13, we are seeing that you are proposing a decree on application of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. But it doesn't say "teritorij." Rather, it says "Ter."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then you're also proposing a decree on the application of the Law on Court Fees. My question, and it's similar to the ones that have been asked before, the Criminal Codes that you proposed and which were enacted, those which in fact adopted the legislation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did that legislation apply to all of the people living in the territory or the area of Herceg-Bosna or only to certain people? How did people know, I guess is my question, how would one know what law he's subject to if he finds himself living in one of the municipalities of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're asking me now is to tell you about the application of the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the application of the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you're asking me which territory it's applicable to, do you not? The Criminal Code of the SFRY was applicable throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and all the republics of that former republic adopted it. The Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina was applicable throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the areas of the HZ HB and the areas under the control of the BH Army. In other words, across the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, without any exceptions, and please allow me to finish my answer. Had I written in this decree that this is applicable to Croats, I would most probably be accused of being an individual adopting discriminatory regulations. Had I written that it applied to Muslims only, the same thing would happen. I did not use the term "drzavljanin" because this does not apply to "drzavljanin." The HZ HB did not have "drzavljanin," nationals. I didn't say that it's applicable only to Croats or only to Muslims because it would be discriminatory. The term opted for was "gradjani" and it was applied across the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina because we adopted it as such and applied it as such. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's time for the break. Can we have the break now, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine with me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer, we have an hour left. You have used up 3 hours and 13 [Realtime transcript read in error "30"] minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a mistake in the transcript. I said 3 hours and 13 minutes, 1-3, not 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, you have in front of you Exhibit -- don't have it in front of me -- it's the minutes of the meeting of the 14th of August, 1992. I don't think you need to go to it in the document, there is a reference in this document then to the appointment of Dr. Jadranko Prlic to be the president of the HVO, is that what occurred also at this Presidency meeting in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He had been in the position of minister or head of the finance department and at that point, then, he was relieved of his duties in the finance department and assumed the position as president of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did he remain in that position, then, for the remainder of the time that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was in existence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the next Presidency meeting that occurred after this one on the 14th of August took place in October, on the 17th of October, 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you about that meeting and the Presidency but before we do that I'm going to ask you if you recall going to Zagreb on the 17th or on or about the 17th of September, 1992, you and others from Bosnia-Herzegovina, going to Zagreb and meeting with President Tudjman in the presidential palace there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Including the extended delegation that accompanied the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in your binder, and I'm going to refer to -- this is a presidential transcript, Mr. President, but I'm going to refer to the Defence version of it because it has additional translation. That's 1D 02366, which is in binder number 4. Just a couple of questions about this meeting in Zagreb, Mr. Buntic. You testified about this transcript earlier in your direct examination, I believe. I think you indicated that you were not aware that the meeting was being tape recorded.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I testified to that. I was also shown the document. I talked about my discussions at the meeting. It is also true that I didn't know that a transcript was being made and that the meeting was being tape recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the heading of this document, and the first opening comments of President Tudjman that are found on the first page, indicate that this is -- it's a meeting of a somewhat political nature in that it involves the leadership or the representatives of the HDZ party, Croatian Democratic Union, but also involves members such as yourself of the Croatian Democratic Party, if I put that correctly.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's roughly the case, although the introductory part was not quoted fully but that's the general gist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I guess the point is that these are delegations of political parties as opposed to delegations of a different state. That's my --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, [Interpretation] My apologies, I'd better turn to Croatian. I believe that the translation of the first paragraph where the president greets those attendees is quite wrong because in the English, as my learned friend rightly mentioned, HDH, the Croatian Democratic Community is also mentioned. Something is wrong there. But in the Croatian text there is -- or, rather, there is the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, but no other party is mentioned. Whereas in the English language it seems as if the representatives of two parties were being introduced here. I'm not sure, though. We would have to look into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I don't think it's important to my questions, Mr. President. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise but I do believe this is important because otherwise my learned friend would not have said in his question that representatives of the political parties gathered here. I can read this again in Croatian and the interpreters can interpret the first sentence below the headline, "Minutes." So that we avoid any confusion. So it says, "Minutes from the meeting of the state and political leadership of Croatia, the meeting of the state and political leadership of Croatia, with the representatives of the Croatian Democratic Union, and Croat representatives from Bosnia and Herzegovina, held in Zagreb on the 17th of September, 1992." It is quite clear that there is just one political party and that Croat representatives are mentioned, and not other parties. And the same is true for the following paragraph below the word "president."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I'd like to direct you to the part of the transcript that includes your own comments which I believe are found on page 33 of your version, page 16 of the English. 16. And you begin to speak, Mr. Buntic, here, and I mentioned this yesterday. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Stringer, could you assist us? My copy here jumps from 13 to 21. And at 21 is then 21 out of 100 whereas the first 13 pages do not refer to out of 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, what's happened here is we've had -- Defence have gotten translations of passages which were not translated previously and those are inserted among the existing translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you go after page 30, Your Honour, you'll find that after page 30 you have page 14 inserted and then 15 and 16. So first go to page 30, it will take you then to page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It may be more useful or in addition I'm just looking at the very -- the Bates number at the bottom which appears to be continuous, 1D 52-1090 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- is the page I'm referring to in the English version. 1090.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I asked you about this yesterday. The language in the preamble, in the amended decision on establishing Herceg-Bosna, that passage about the unacceptability of a unitary state in a multi-ethnic society, and it seems to me that again we are finding those very same words here, you're again expressing the view that -- if I can interpret it correctly, that you do not accept or do not approve of a unitary principle as applied to a multi-ethnic community. Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. However, the introductory part of your question is not correct, and I kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to rectify it. I have never said that I am against a multi-ethnic society. This is, however, what follows from the first part of your question. Everything that is written here, and everything I said, is something that I still maintain. However, I'm not going to stand by something that you're trying to impute to me in your question. It is true that I said that I was against a unitary state system in which there are multi-ethnic societies. This is something that comes -- stems from the Bosnia-Herzegovinian constitution, the SFRY constitution, the UN charter, and many other documents. I do stand by what I said here but do not impute to me or let me go so far as to say that you're trying to put words that I never uttered into my mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, there must be a problem in interpretation because the English makes it quite clear that the Prosecutor did not in any way impute any such opinion to you. So you can be assured that nothing like that can be read from the transcript. It must be a problem of translation or understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. That was the interpretation I received. I don't know if that was the case with the others who were listening to Croatian interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Buntic, I'm not suggesting that you're opposed to a multi-ethnic society. I am suggesting based on the text here, and I think you've confirmed it, that you believe that the unitary state model is not an appropriate model or is not the best model to apply to a multi-ethnic society. Is that a correct statement of your view?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now your question is correct and I can answer with a yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Turning the page of the English version, and I'm not sure if it's on the next page of your version, Mr. Buntic, I'm skipping down to a paragraph in which you say that: "In addition to this, well-known facts which can easily be calculated by using statistics, the decreasing number of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, such as it was, because of the large number of Croats who have moved out and also because of the Muslims moving into Bosnia and Herzegovina, such as it is, and the fact of the establishment of an Independent State of Croatia, the Republic of Croatia, if Bosnia-Herzegovina is arranged as a unitary state, I believe that the percentage of the Croats moving out because now they have their own state to which they would go, and the Muslims from Sandzak and Kosovo moving in would at least double." And then you go on to talk about configuring Bosnia-Herzegovina as a complex state. And I just want to ask you about your statement there, Mr. Buntic, because I recognise that you have the view that that unitary state model does not work for a multi-ethnic society, am I correct that that view which you hold is based upon the demographic composition of Bosnia-Herzegovina and perhaps the trends that you're referring to here in which Croats may be on the move out or that their numbers are diminishing whereas the numbers of the Bosniak or Muslim population are increasing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you are right. However, I am right as well, unfortunately. Allow me to finish my answer. If you read carefully the minutes from the meetings of the Croatian Defence Council, HVO, dating from the period immediately preceding this one, you will see that the HVO charged me with -- along with Mr. Markotic, who was a demographer by profession, to make an analysis of the trends in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We went back a hundred years and we looked at the more recent period. On the basis of the data thus gathered, we were supposed to submit a report to the HVO. I contacted Professor Dr. Markotic, a demographer, who studied that issue. Now, why did I say unfortunately I was right? I have documentation, some of it even in my bag, showing that there are 300.000 fewer Croats than there were in 1993. This is the information published also in the -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina by an international agency. Therefore, some 40 -- the total number of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina has fallen by 40 per cent compared to 1991, whereas, in the part -- if we look at all the censuses that were conducted in the past 100 years, every subsequent census recorded a fewer number of Croats. In other words, this becomes a sort of a tenet or a rule, and the HZ HB had to formulate a policy on the basis of that. Unfortunately, all the events transpiring in Bosnia-Herzegovina led to the fact that 300.000 Croats were either driven out, killed or left Bosnia-Herzegovina of their own free will because, as I said here as well, the fact that the Republic of Croatia was -- became independent was something that would result in the number of Croats being reduced three times due to emigration, unfortunately. Something that I said at the time that unless Croats had their own area, I will not use the term territory --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In fact, I've read the minutes of the HVO meetings in which you and Mr. Markotic were given the responsibility of preparing the demographic reports, and I will be showing those to you. I do have them prepared and we will be looking at those. I am aware of that. And so I apologise for cutting you off but I can do that with the assurance that you will have the minutes in front of you and we'll give you a full opportunity to talk about the demographic issue. For the moment, though, I think that you've given us enough on the subject to allow me to ask the next question or two that I have in respect of the transcript here. Given the view, your findings, that over time the Croatian population of Bosnia-Herzegovina is diminishing, am I correct in suggesting, sir, that your own view, in terms of an appropriate model of governance in Bosnia-Herzegovina, is one in which any of the groups, Croat, Muslim, Serb, should have an area in which it can govern itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there needs to be a precision. They are not groups, they are constituent nations and there lies the issue with Mr. Buntic's previous answer, because we are not talking about a minority, a national minority, we are talking about a constituent nation so I would ask that my learned colleague refer to them as constituent nations and not as groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, I'm happy to do that, Mr. President. I think we all need to know what constituent means because we hear the word a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's in the constitution. It's in the constitution, we should refer to the constitution. It's always been there. Has been there, still is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Given that the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina were a constituent nation, given the demographic trends in which their numbers were diminishing, is it your view that the Croatian people should have had an area that they could govern themselves so that they wouldn't have to be worried about being outvoted all the time by another group, by another constituent nation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I answered such questions in the course of my evidence, and I entirely stand by what I said so far. Let me only clarify something that I started explaining but was then interrupted. I still maintain my view. However, I cannot speak about what other people thought or wanted. What I can say is that to the Presidency of the HVO, and its leadership, all the peace plans proposed by the international community were acceptable. Through its decisions, the Presidency clearly expressed its views. These were views held by the official bodies of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. As you were able to see, I expressed my opinion on several occasions which does not mean that this opinion was shared by the entire Presidency and the official bodies. It was mine. And I stand by it. The official opinions and views were expressed through official documents and were manifested as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, continuing on in the transcript, in your comments you continue -- I'm looking at the top of the following page, 18 or the page which ends in the numbers 1092. You state, "Further I will present my view of Bosnia and Herzegovina which, as I say, is also contested." So I -- you're being candid or you are conceding that your views are not shared by all. "I hold that regardless of the international recognition of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is not a state but a state which is only just coming into being. When I say coming into being, I explain it by the fact that it is partly occupied, that its government bodies and I primarily mean the assembly do not function, do not exist. If we know that what makes a state are territory and jurisdiction, i.e., authority over a particular territory, then we can easily conclude that at the moment, Bosnia and Herzegovina does not exist as a sovereign state in most of its territory." Now, the Trial Chamber knows that large parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina were occupied by the JNA during this period of time. The Trial Chamber also knows about the inability or as the -- the constraints that were in effect in terms of the central government in Sarajevo, particularly the fact that the Serbs were not participating in the assembly, so we don't need to talk about that. My question, then, is as follows: Given that state of affairs as you describe here regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it your view then that that situation was one in which, provided an opportunity for the Croatian people to make a space for itself as a constituent nation which it could govern? If there was a void in governance based on the conditions, that you and others perhaps proposed to fill that void by creating a constituent unit of the Croatian people in territory which Croatian people would govern?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, your question is correct or proper, with the exception of the part where you say that the Croatian people would govern. So, yes, but I would just like to clarify one thing that is used in various expressions and terms. This shows an effort, an effort to bring Bosnia-Herzegovina together, not to divide it, because it was broken apart, 70 per cent of it was occupied, it was under the power of the enemy, of the enemy armed force. It didn't function in 70 per cent of its territory. Its bodies were not functioning, the assembly was not functioning, the government was not functioning. The Presidency, well, we've already said, Izetbegovic had three or four terms of office whereas under the law he could only have two. So the government bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina functioned in 10 per cent or so of its territory. So all the efforts were not to divide the country but to bring it back together, to put it together again on the basis of this constitutional structure. So this was not a division. This was putting things back together, because 70 per cent was already gone. It was in the hands of the occupying force. And we have seen, I told you what the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina was doing while this occupation was taking place, while there were those fierce attacks. The Presidency officially invited the Yugoslav People's Army, the occupying force, to intervene. So something had to be done and parts of the territory of that state had to be saved. I have told you what the Presidency was doing. I can give you the transcript from a session of the Presidency, in April, the Yugoslav People's Army is called upon to intervene in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The enemy armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: As I've indicated the Trial Chamber has heard a great deal of evidence about those events and I don't think we need to take time to talk about them so much now. I'm simply asking you what in your view was the appropriate response and how it impacted the way in which Herceg-Bosna was being organised. Now, getting back to the transcript I'd like to skip ahead a few pages because in this meeting, you did something that I thought was rather courageous, given that you're attending a meeting of the -- with the president of Croatia, who also happened to be the leader of the Croatian Democratic Union for Croatia and that you were surrounded by other members of the Croatian Democratic Party both for Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, even though you weren't one yourself, because at the end of your comments you criticize the HDZ leadership for its failure to propose a platform earlier. And I'm looking at page 20 of the English version. You can skip ahead, Mr. Buntic, if you can follow along with me, I'm going to move ahead a few pages to the part where the president says, "Wait, let Mr. Buntic finish. And then you may ask to speak." And what you'll see is just in the preceding paragraph, that's you talking, and you say, "As for not having had a platform until now, I think that somebody else is responsible for that and now I must say what hurt me deeply as a Croat. It hurt me that six or eight months ago while discussing the platforms of the SDS and the SDA, the communists, reformists, the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina never presented its own platform." Then there is an interjection. And President Tudjman allows you to finish speaking and we then pass to a statement by Mr. Vlado Pandzic on the following page. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it, and Mr. Prosecutor, this is an integral part of Mr. Zoran Buntic's character. That's just who I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll accept that. What Mr. Pandzic says is this. He says, "Right at the start I would refute Mr. Buntic's words. The HDZ platform was agreed on, clear, articulated with the headquarters in Zagreb. I think that you are also familiar with it, Mr. President. So I have to refute this in order to avoid further misunderstanding." He continues, "We emphasise this strongly and clearly. The Croatian people must be sovereign in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Its territories must be sovereign and the Croatian people must never again be 'equal to other ethnic groups,' as it used to be said in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Then he continues on, I'm skipping a paragraph. "However, I would return to what our goals are, following from this platform. We have talked about security and securing Croatian territories and the sovereignty of Croatian territories as well as the Croatian people in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Then he continues, "Today we can talk about what is possible to achieve and what we have been emphasizing all the time." I'm going to skip a few words, "I think, and now I will state my personal opinion, that it is possible to achieve what has been -- what was discussed, that the Croatian territories, bearing in mind what the Croatian Banovina included, but we also said that we would take care to secure the Croatian corridors as well. These are the areas where many Croats live and sovereignty should be emphasised there, at least in the form of a Croatian municipality" and I'm going to stop there. He continues talking about Croatian constitutive units in which Croatian population would be in the majority. Now, Mr. Buntic, my question is this: Is it -- am I correct, then, to understand here that what is the objective of the HDZ party as being described by Mr. Pandzic is the establishment of Croatian territory, sovereign Croatian territory, where it's governed by Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you could see, I cannot confirm everything that you said. But here, this man, Vlado Pandzic is saying those things. He mentions the Croatian Banovina, so this was part of the reasons why I had conflicts with him, because my opinions differed from his. But, yes, I still maintain what I said. It is correct, despite what he is saying, that the platform was never presented. I'm not going to say in public but at the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, where it should have been dealt with, because it voted on proposals of the SDA and the SDS but it never voted on the proposals of the HDZ in the assembly. That was the relevant place, that's where it was supposed to be debated. And this was the gist of my criticism to the then leadership of the HDZ. Well, regardless of the fact that President Boban and President Tudjman were there and other officials. I said this is the way I am, I presented my opinion, it was my opinion at the time, and it has remained unchanged. It is still my opinion and I still stand behind everything that I said. And as you can see, I clashed with the people who presented different views, despite the fact that all of them were in the HDZ, I was probably the only non-party partisan person there. I may be wrong there, so I do at apologise in advance, maybe there were other people who were not members of the HDZ there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It seems to me in one respect you agree with the views expressed by Mr. Pandzic here in that the Croatian people must be sovereign in Bosnia-Herzegovina, its territories must be sovereign and the Croatian people must never again be equal to other groups which as I take it to be a rejection again of this unitary state model. Isn't it your view as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. That was my opinion then, and it is still my opinion and I never deviated from it. I confirmed this on a number of occasions in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honours, but perhaps there is a -- again some communication problem that has to do with interpretation or translation. I don't know whether the witness has the Croatian version of this text in front of him but in the Croatian version of this text that is being quoted, where Mr. Pandzic is being quoted in the second paragraph, the words "equal to other peoples" is in inverted commas and I think it really changes the meaning. I think that the witness should look at it and then try to recall what this is all about. I don't know whether there are the inverted commas in the English version -- yes, yes, they are in inverted commas and it this has not been stressed and this is very important because perhaps the witness might explain to us what it means in Bosnia-Herzegovina when you put the word "equal" in inverted commas from the perspective of the Croatian people at that time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the inverted commas are in both texts. I just don't think it's productive to have a committee of people interjecting comments on how questioning should take place. I read it, I indicated when I read it that there was a quotation mark. The text was in front of the witness as he followed along so it seems rather pointless to me to make such an intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask counsel the following question: In the B/C/S version, where -- on which page can we find those inverted commas? Witness, you told us that you didn't know that the meeting was recorded so there was a recording system in place for the whole meeting, maybe there was a tape recorder or something. The meeting is recorded. And then some clerk, some typist, transcribes what has been said. So how did the secretary insert inverted commas? How come? This is a mystery to me. Can you provide us with an explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, I would find it really hard to explain how somebody who typed up this transcript or who did the transcription on the basis of the audio recording, how this whole technology worked, but -- that I don't know. But I can tell you what I do know, and what I do know for a fact is that it is true, again let me remind you I can tell you things about what I said, and my words that are recorded in the transcript, it is true that most of my words, my thoughts, are recorded verbatim in the transcript, but it is also true that not all of the things that I said are recorded. I know that for a fact. Now, as to what happened to the other participants in the discussion, whether what they were saying is recorded verbatim or not, I cannot testify to that, because that I don't know. And as to how this was done in terms of technology and the methodology, how the audio recordings were transformed into the hard copy that we have in front of us, I'm afraid that I could lead you astray in this if I were to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak attended those meetings. Maybe he can shed some light on that matter. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] When you're saying something, when you come to the part that you want to put in inverted comma, every speaker would say, "in inverted commas." And then the words, "in inverted commas" were not recorded in the transcript but the inverted commas were placed around the portion of the text that was supposed to be in inverted commas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That could be an explanation, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, on this page 38, I have looked for a -- for the word, "teritorij" which I did not find. I find "prostor." Would that be an equivalent and how would that fall to be translated? I hope I'm not stepping on your toes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, not at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see this. Your Honour, the word used here is "prostor," space or area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. Buntic, now, as I understand it, then, you held the view, it's a view expressed by Mr. Pandzic here in relation to a sovereign area or space that's governed by Croatian people. That was the objective, that was the aspiration. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, well, I can't answer this question if you're talking about an area where the Croatian people enjoyed the sovereignty, I never said that this area would be ruled or governed exclusively by the Croatian people. So please do not impute this to me. That was not said. In that area, the Croatian people should have a majority in the area of this constituent unit and there are no proposals that would be different from other solutions that were presented in the Yugoslav constitution because every republic in the former Yugoslavia had the main people but also other peoples living there. And the participation in the government would be commensurate to their participation in the overall number. We know that Serbia was divided, that the Republic of Serbia had two autonomous provinces, that there was a certain number of delegates from Vojvodina and from Kosovo who participated in the work of the central bodies of the government of Serbia, and in other republics, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in principle, it functioned in this way. The executive bodies were set up in such a way that each people was represented by one person. And we were now at a stage where it was being sought and, as I said, we did not encounter this in our practice, that a multi-ethnic community would be set up as a unitary state based on the principle of one man/one vote. This is my opinion. I don't have to clarify that any further. This was an unacceptable principle that resulted in the war in Yugoslavia and we all know that this principle was advocated by Milosevic and that he got himself in conflict with all the other republics because he advocated this principle and this is why Yugoslavia broke up. Dissolution resulted from that, and the bloody war and all the other consequences of the war. The final result being the collapse of that state because this principle, one man/one vote, a unitary civil state, was being imposed. I think that I clarified everything. I also presented my own views, my own opinions, but I agreed with all the decisions, I accepted all the decisions, that were taken by the elected representatives of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, when they accepted the Cutileiro Plan, the Vance-Owen Plan, so whenever -- when I participated in the executive body, that was duty-bound to implement what the authorised bodies accepted and signed. And now we are talking about our opinions, and this is my opinion, and it is accurately recorded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'm simply asking your opinion, what were your views, and as I understand it, then, your view, your opinion, I used the word governance, that was a word that you did not accept, Croatian or Croat governance. You came back and said a majority. So then do I take it that what -- your view was that there should be an area in which Croatian people would be in the majority, I take it also an area in which Muslim people could be in the majority and another area in which the Serbian people could be in the majority. Is that your view of an acceptable model of governance within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. The next exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Stringer. I wouldn't like to put a question to the witness but to Mr. Stringer. A while ago I heard what the witness said regarding the transcript. He stated that the transcript reflected what he said but that some of the things he said did not appear in the transcript. Therefore, the transcript does not reflect fully what was said during that meeting. The Trial Chamber admitted a few transcripts, as you well know, and therefore I have this question in mind. When you asked the Croatian authorities to disclose the presidential transcripts, were you given the audiotapes too?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is an area in which I feel as though I'm probably not the best person to answer the Trial Chamber's questions on the acquisition of these materials from the Croatian government. So I think just to be on the safe side, I should seek out the information to make sure I give the right answers to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be of assistance, to answer this question, instead of my colleague, I know that those transcripts were obtained by the Prosecution and were disclosed to the Defence teams and this whole process started in the summer of 2000, and then it proceeded slowly from there. But as regards the technology, how the recordings were made, there are three witnesses who testified about that in the Kordic case so if you're interested in it, you can ask for that proprio motu. And it also follows from the testimony in the Kordic case that the audio recordings do not exist. This was the topic of the testimony, and the Prosecution called those witnesses. So it's very easy to obtain this, and I don't think that the Defence has any interest in doing that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please let us know whenever possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We will do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, the next document on my list, I don't know if it's necessary for you to look at it, but perhaps, it's in the binder, P 00476. This is in the binder number 2. And this was already the subject of, I think, a question from Judge Trechsel earlier today. This is the constitutional court decision of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And you've indicated that you weren't aware of this or you hadn't seen this decision and so I don't think there is very much for me to ask you about it. If I understand correctly, sir, you did not become aware of this decision until some years after it was issued?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct, Your Honours, although in the meantime I talked to some of the Judges on the constitutional court who issued this decision or took part in making this decision, and they never informed me about its existence, they never handed it to me. To be quite specific, I said that in December 1992, between the 19th and the 23rd of December, I spoke in Neum with a judge of this Court, Kasim Trnka. At the time he was in fact the president of the Court, and he never told me about this decision, about its very existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And the judge of the Court whom you spoke with, excuse me, in Neum in December, he was a judge based in Sarajevo then, with the constitutional court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure where he was from, but let us assume that he was from Sarajevo, that he lived in Sarajevo, because he was a judge of the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina that had its seat in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I know you were asked about this issue when you testified in the Kordic case and it was my understanding that you didn't see this decision until later because you were not in a position to be receiving the Official Gazettes of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because I think in the decision that you have in front of you, you have the version that is -- actually forms a part of the Official Gazettes and so you were not receiving those during this period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and we couldn't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And is that because of the --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was physically impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because of the situation in Sarajevo, that it was under siege, if you will, by the forces of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, can you recall, when you -- when it was no longer possible to physically receive the Official Gazettes of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 4th or the 5th of April, 1992, or immediately after that day, we were no longer able to receive the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If it did happen, then it happened because somebody was able to get out of Sarajevo by some channels and was able to bring a couple of copies of the Official Gazette with him or her. So there was this possibility. I know that it did happen from time to time, but officially, by mail, it was not possible to receive the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, is it time for the break or the end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I just have one very brief follow-up question. I understand very well what the situation was, but given the importance of that decision, a lawyer in Sarajevo could have made a phone call in order to say that the constitutional court had issued an important decision. Was there no telephone communication between Sarajevo and Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no. There was no telephone communication, no mail. Now, I can't really say with full certainty that there was not some kind of dedicated military line of communication using field telephones, but official phones and mail were not working because all the telephone exchanges were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is now 7.00 p.m. We need to adjourn. I inform the Prosecution that it has used up four hours. It would be good if you could finish tomorrow, so that on Friday, we can have redirect and maybe questions put by the other Defence teams. Therefore, the witness will be able to go. Otherwise, he will have to stay some three weeks. Witness, we shall reconvene tomorrow at quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th of July, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
